strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: identifies the critical trade-off between typographic robustness and text-reading ability, revealing a fundamental misalignment in existing evaluation paradigms
Elegant benchmark design with same-scene counterfactuals: the orthogonal taxonomy (object vs. text questions × clean vs. attacked) enables controlled, confound-free evaluation within identical scenes
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 6 diverse LVLMs, multiple defense strategies, thorough ablations (attack levels, LoRA placement, data size), and generalization studies to external datasets

Technically sound construction pipeline: principled attack generation with hierarchical difficulty levels, OCR-aware placement to avoid trivial overlaps, and efficient implementation (3 hours for full dataset construction)
Strong reproducibility: detailed 18-page supplementary material, promise to release data-generation code enabling flexible dataset resampling, comprehensive implementation details

Clear architectural insights: Table 2 reveals that selective text use is primarily learned through language model reasoning rather than vision encoder modifications, contradicting prior vision-centric defenses
Well-written presentation with effective motivation: Figures 1 and 3 clearly communicate the problem and solution; practical relevance to autonomous vehicles and embodied AI systems
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: RIO-RT is straightforward balanced SFT on mixed object/text-attack data—a 'correct' training strategy rather than a novel defense mechanism; missing deeper analysis of why balanced training works

Scope constraints: evaluation limited to VQA tasks; no real-world deployment validation despite claims about autonomous vehicles; benchmark instantiated on TextVQA only, though pipeline is generalizable in principle

Generalization concerns: Table 4 shows domain-specific behavior (e.g., Llama-3.2-Vision IT-RT degrades RIO-Bench text reading but preserves external text-VQA performance), suggesting learned capability may not transfer broadly beyond scene text

Text-attack generation questions: LLM-based attack generation may introduce predictable patterns; OCR-based key text identification could fail on handwritten/stylized text; grid-based distance placement may not reflect naturalistic attack distributions

Modest improvement margins: RIO-RT gains over IT-RT on Text-Attack are often modest (8-9% for several models); raises questions about whether balanced training is minimal sufficient intervention or if more sophisticated approaches could yield better trade-offs

Missing error analysis and statistical testing: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing; no detailed failure case analysis for RIO-RT; some percentage changes small enough to warrant formal significance testing
Ambiguous ground truth not discussed: some scenarios are genuinely ambiguous (e.g., misleading text in generic image descriptions); no treatment of annotation confidence or model disagreement cases

Benchmark scope: 21,953 training images is reasonable but modest; no analysis of whether performance plateaus or would benefit from larger data; generalization to non-VQA multimodal reasoning tasks (instruction following, visual reasoning) unexplored
